notes: Account overview: large fintech vertical with high-frequency personalization and chat support workflows. Very latency-sensitive for customer-facing flows; heavy compliance requirements (EU + NA data residency).
Primary ask: Dedicated capacity with throughput guarantees for peak trading-hour traffic and an SLA that is explicit about tail latency measurements (p95/p99).
Observed constraints: model is a 70B decoder-only variant, KV cache warms slowly across cold starts; they plan to serve both streaming chat and non-streaming batch reranks from same endpoints.
SLO definitions discussed (key snippets):

- p50 / p95 / p99 granularity: customer wants both per-request and per-token metrics for streaming responses. Preference: p95 <= 250ms non-streaming inference; p95 <= 100ms for token-level vs client perceived latency for streaming.

- Measurement origin debate: CTO insists p99 must be client-observed end-to-end (browser -> edge -> model -> first byte) so CDN/edge variability is included. Redwood legal/ops propose server-side measurement for contractual SLA with a separate operational metric for client-side E2E.

- Streaming vs non-streaming: agreed that streaming SLOs will be token-latency-focused (time-to-first-token and inter-token intervals) while non-streaming uses total request completion time. Need clear mapping in contract.
Key technical concerns raised by Cedar engineering team:
- Warmup/warm-cache behavior: p99 spikes on cold starts; want guaranteed warm pools or documented 'warmup' SLAs for capacity burst periods.
- Batching behavior: autoscaling and batching improve throughput and cost but can add tail latency under low QPS — customer wants guidance and safe defaults for batching windows per workload.

- Client-side timers: they will measure end-to-end using an in-house RUM agent. Request: Redwood provide a measurement spec (timestamps to emit, event names) so their RUM can correlate with server traces.
Selected contractual items they asked for:
- Explicit definition: 'p99 latency' = 99th percentile of server-side request-completion time measured at the Redwood-serving ingress point over a 30-day rolling window unless otherwise specified.
- Addendum: client-observed p99 provided as a non-binding operational report for first year; revisit binding after POC if both sides agree on measurement instrumentation.
Proof-of-concept notes:

- POC plan: 2-week POC inside customer VPC with 3 reserved GPUs, synthetic traffic matching their 99th percentile QPS profile. Deliverables: latency histograms (per-token & per-request), KV cache hit rates, batching stats.
- Success criteria brainstormed: p95 <= 250ms non-streaming, p95 token inter-arrival <= 120ms for streaming, end-to-end client p95 within 1.5x of server p95 under steady-state.
Quotes/voice-of-customer: 'We will tolerate some warmup blips but need predictable tail behavior during the 2 hour market open window' — CTO (Daniel Park).
Open technical action items for SE team:
1) Produce 'SLO measurement spec' doc with example traces and timestamp points (client send, edge receive, server ingress, first-token, last-token). Link draft in Drive.
2) Run targeted POC run with and without batching to show tradeoffs; include cold-start simulation and warm-pool baseline.
3) Provide recommended reserved GPU counts for 95% of peak scenarios and LOE for automatic warm pools (cost + config).

Commercial notes: estimated ARR range discussed; customer prefers a committed-reserved model with annual true-ups. They requested SLA language that ties credits to measured server-side availability and documented p99 breaches.
